title: Immunization and Spot Rates
text:
Duration
\[D = \sum_{t} t \cdot \frac{CF_t / (1+y)^t}{P}\]
The present-value-weighted average time to receipt, in years.
For a zero-coupon bond, \(D\) equals maturity. For a coupon bond, \(D\) is less than maturity.

title: Immunization and Spot Rates
section: Modified duration and the price approximation
text:
Modified duration and the price approximation
\[D^* = \frac{D}{1+y}, \qquad \frac{\Delta P}{P} \approx -D^* \times \Delta y\]
A bond with \(D = 7\) and \(y = 4\%\) has \(D^* = 6.73\). A 100 basis point rise in yields gives
\[\frac{\Delta P}{P} \approx -6.73 \times 0.01 = -6.73\%\]

title: Immunization and Spot Rates
text:
Definition
A portfolio of bonds is immunized against a liability when two conditions hold at the same time:


Present value
\[PV_{\text{assets}} = PV_{\text{liability}}\]


Duration
\[D_{\text{assets}} = D_{\text{liability}}\]


Portfolio duration is the value-weighted average of the durations of the holdings.

title: Immunization and Spot Rates
section: What the two conditions do and do not deliver
text:
What the two conditions do and do not deliver


Holds
Small parallel shifts, immediately after the match is struck.


Surplus
Large parallel shifts, when asset convexity exceeds the liability’s.


Deficit
Non-parallel shifts, and the passage of time, since durations drift apart.


Rebalancing is required as time passes and as rates move.

title: From Statements to Free Cash Flow
text:
What each one reports


Income statement
Revenues and expenses over a period, on an accrual basis.


Balance sheet
Assets, liabilities, and equity at a point in time. Two consecutive balance sheets give the change in working capital.


Cash flow statement
Cash received and paid over a period, split into operating, investing, and financing.

title: From Statements to Free Cash Flow
text:
The definition
\[\text{FCFF} = \text{EBIT}(1-t) + \text{D\&A} - \text{CapEx} - \Delta \text{NWC}\]
Cash generated by operations after reinvestment, before any payment to debt or equity holders.

title: From Statements to Free Cash Flow
text:
Two routes to one number


From the income statement
\(\text{EBIT}(1-t)\)
\(+\ \text{D\&A}\)
\(-\ \text{CapEx}\)
\(-\ \Delta \text{NWC}\)

From the cash flow statement
\(\text{Cash from operations}\)
\(+\ \text{Interest}(1-t)\)
\(-\ \text{CapEx}\)

Equal only after reconciling non-cash items.

title: From Statements to Free Cash Flow
text:
Why they disagree


Non-cash charges you forgot
Stock compensation, impairments, deferred taxes.


Working capital, redefined
The cash flow statement’s version is not the balance sheet’s.


Leases
Operating lease treatment changes both EBIT and capital expenditure.


Acquisitions
Reinvestment reported separately from capital expenditure.

title: Course Overview
text:
Best practices — structure


Every assumption gets its own labeled cell, in one block at the top
Formulas reference those cells, never a number typed inside the formula
The same formula runs across every period of a projection
Every hardcoded number carries its source beside it



Write =B5*(1+$B$6), not =B5*1.05. Source format: document, date, specific reference — “Company 10-K, FY2025, page 45, revenue note.”

title: Course Overview
text:
Best practices — presentation







Convention
Rule




Blue text
Hardcoded inputs — the cells a reader is meant to change


Black text
Every formula and calculation


Green text
Links to another sheet in the same workbook


Currency
$#,##0, with units in the header: Revenue ($mm)


Percentages
One decimal. Valuation multiples as 0.0x


Negatives
Parentheses, (123), not −123



Zero formula errors on delivery: no #REF!, #DIV/0!, #VALUE!, or #NAME?.

title: Course Overview
text:
Why the colors matter


The color convention is not decoration. It is how a reader knows, at a glance, what they are allowed to change.


For your reader
Blue says “this is an assumption, argue with it.” Black says “this follows from the assumptions, do not touch it.”

Three things that will trip you up

The file browser does not notice a new file on its own. Use the refresh button above it.

Download to open
Workbooks come down to your laptop through the three-dots menu, and open in your own Excel.

title: Course Overview
section: The large language model (LLM) only writes text
text:
The large language model (LLM) only writes text

The model cannot open a file, run a calculation, or fetch a filing. It reads text and writes text. That is the entire capability.

What makes it useful is the harness around it. The model emits a request to use a tool; the harness runs the tool and reports the result back.

title: Course Overview
text:
The loop


The harness sends the prompt, the conversation, and the list of tools
The model answers: use tool X, with these arguments
The harness runs X and reports the result back
The model decides what comes next — another tool, or an answer for you



On the lab, GLM writes a Python file, runs it at the terminal, reads the output, and revises. Four tool calls before you see anything.

title: Course Overview
text:
Claude inside Excel

There are also Claude, ChatGPT, and CoPilot plugins for Excel , from Home → Add-ins. The chat window sits inside the workbook.



They need paid accounts or particular types of license agreements. We will not use them.

title: Course Overview
text:
Plan before you act
For any complex operation, ask AI to plan first, or ask it what the best way is to do something, before it begins to work.


Planning pulls the knowledge in
Plan how you will do this before you start. The plan puts the relevant considerations into the conversation, and it answers in light of those rather than from base rates.


Planning breaks the work up
Steps you can check one at a time. Failures stay small and local instead of surfacing at the end, when everything downstream is already wrong.

title: Course Overview
text:
Misunderstandings and bad assumptions


The problem
Errors usually come from

AI misunderstood what you wanted, or
The task could be done in multiple ways, you did not specify, and AI chose the wrong path



What to say:

Tell me what you are about to do
Tell me what you did
Was there any ambiguity in my instructions? Did you make any choices we did not discuss?

title: Course Overview
text:
Numbers need code

AI has gotten better at arithmetic, but it is still not to be trusted at math — it is trained to predict language
Always ask it to run code if you need a number
It may not be good at predicting what should follow “what is 32 times 17?” but it is very good at generating code “x = 32 * 17; print(x)”

title: Course Overview
section: Ask why your idea is bad, not why it is good
text:
Ask why your idea is bad, not why it is good
Training on human feedback teaches that agreement earns high ratings. Ask “is this valuation sound?” and it will find reasons that it is.

Invert it. What is the strongest argument that this project should be rejected?

title: Course Overview
text:
Use independent agents as critics


AI is not a good self-critic
Ask AI in the same conversation to evaluate its work. It will review its own reasoning and conclude it is sound.


Start a new conversation or ask for a subagent
A new conversation or a subagent will not see the prior reasoning. It will look at it “with a fresh set of eyes.”

title: Course Overview
text:
Hallucinations

Hallucinations are much less frequent now than a few years ago
Hallucinating code is really not an issue
Ask for web search and a source for any fact
The greatest risk is asking for an obscure fact that it cannot find via a web search

title: Course Overview
text:
Verify and retain code


Check the outputs
We don’t usually check AI code by reading it. We check small cases where we can verify “by hand” (using AI to help with that too).


And keep what works
Keep code that has been vetted. Tell AI to use it again the next time.

title: Bond Pricing and Duration
section: A bond is a promise with a date on it
text:
A bond is a promise with a date on it


Coupon
Fixed cash on fixed dates. Contractual, not discretionary.


Principal
Face value, repaid at maturity.


Yield
Not a promise. The rate that makes today’s price equal the discounted promises.

title: Bond Pricing and Duration
text:
One rate is not enough
\[P = \sum_{t=1}^{T} \frac{C}{(1+r_t)^t} + \frac{F}{(1+r_T)^T}\]
Each cash flow is discounted at the rate for its own maturity. The set of rates \(r_1, \ldots, r_T\) is the term structure.

title: Bond Pricing and Duration
section: Lab 1 — price one off the curve
text:
Lab 1 — price one off the curve
Spot rates for maturities 1 through 10 are on the handout.


Lay out the ten cash flows of a 10-year 4% annual coupon bond
Discount each at the spot rate for its own maturity, and sum
Find the single yield that produces the same price



Report the price and that yield.

title: Bond Pricing and Duration
text:
Interest rate risk
A bond’s price falls when yields rise. The size of the fall depends on the timing of the cash flows, not on maturity alone.
A 10-year 8% coupon bond returns cash earlier than a 10-year zero, and its price moves less for the same change in yield.

title: Bond Pricing and Duration
text:
Duration
\[D = \frac{\sum_t t \cdot w_t}{\sum_t w_t}, \qquad w_t = \frac{CF_t}{(1+y)^t}\]
The average date on which you get your money, weighted by present value.
\[\frac{\Delta P}{P} \approx -\frac{D}{1+y} \times \Delta y\]

title: Bond Pricing and Duration
text:
Lab 2 — predict, then check


Compute the bond’s duration from the same spreadsheet
Predict the price change for a 100 bp rise, using \(-D^* \times \Delta y\)
Reprice at the higher yields and compare



Post two numbers: the predicted price change and the actual one.

title: Bond Pricing and Duration
text:
Accuracy of the approximation
The formula is a first-order approximation: it uses the slope of the price-yield relation at the current yield.
The price-yield relation is convex, so the actual price exceeds the linear estimate for both increases and decreases in yield. The error grows with the size of the yield change.
